title: Frequently asked questions
subtitle: We deal early with details that may seem insignificant at first but can turn into problems over time.

items.q: We already have a distributor in Brazil. Why should we speak to you as well?
items.a: Because your distributor shows you the orders they place, but those orders tell you little about how your product reaches the end customer: its shelf price, its positioning, where it is sold and whether the offer is consistent across channels. At the moment, the person giving you this information is the very person whose performance you are assessing. We offer an independent view, particularly useful before you renew the agreement, review exclusivity or give notice to end it.

items.q: Working with a distributor or agent costs us nothing upfront. Why pay for an analysis?
items.a: Because the cost is there even if you do not see it. The distributor earns a margin and the agent earns on sales volume. Each is entitled to work in their own interests. The question worth asking is this: if you are not paying, who is, and whose interests are being served? You alone pay us, so we work solely in your interests, even when our advice is to stay out of the market, change partners or leave.

items.q: Why pay for something that others offer for free?
items.a: Because they offer something different. Public agencies, chambers of commerce and associations offer general information, events and introductions, often free of charge or at little cost. These are useful resources. Make the most of them. They are funded to serve all businesses on the same terms, which is why their guidance remains general. Their role does not extend to helping you decide which partner to choose, how much it would cost to exit a contract, or whether you would be better off staying out of the market. That is where our work begins. We also help you get more out of what you have already obtained for free, whether that is a trade fair, a trade mission or a list of contacts.

items.q: We have neither the time nor the staff to devote to Brazil.
items.a: You do not need to set either aside. We do the work on the ground. We set out the options, their pros and cons, and our recommendation. The decision is yours. Doing nothing is always one of the options, and we set out its costs too, because postponing a decision is itself a choice.

items.q: We have already paid for studies that led nowhere.
items.a: That is a common experience, so we do not ask you to take our word for it. Before we start, you know in writing what we will deliver, when and for what fee. None of the professional firms pays us a commission, and each bills you directly. You receive options with their pros and cons, together with a reasoned recommendation that goes beyond a list of figures.

items.q: What do you need from us?
items.a: The starting information: your product, your objectives, your margins and the resources you can commit. We take it from there.

items.q: Doesn’t the person who draws up the options end up influencing the choice?
items.a: Yes. Anyone who puts the options together influences the choice. That is why it matters who pays them. Only you pay us, and we draw up the options in your interests, including the one that brings us no further work.

items.q: What happens if we decide against a check you recommend?
items.a: It is your decision, and we respect it. We explain in writing why we think the check matters and what skipping it could mean. If you decide to go ahead without it, we ask you to confirm that in writing so everyone is clear about the decision.

items.q: Does checking on the distributor in stores suggest that we do not trust them?
items.a: No. The purpose is to give you another perspective when making a decision: the end customer’s. And if your distributor is doing a good job, what would it cost you to check?

items.q: Why do you work only with specialist firms and not with large firms?
items.a: Because we want the person who signs off on the work to be the one who does it. Each firm covers a single area, and the firms cross-check one another’s work.

items.q: Once the decision has been made, who will implement it?
items.a: It depends on the decision: renegotiating with your distributor, bringing in a professional firm or switching channels. Implementation is a separate assignment, with its own scope and fee agreed in writing beforehand. You can entrust it to us or go ahead on your own.

items.q: How much will it cost us?
items.a: You will know before we start because the fee is set out in our proposal. It is also worth asking what you stand to gain and what a mistake could cost you: the wrong exclusive agreement, a trade mark filed by someone else or an exit whose costs you have not worked out.

items.q: Who pays BMG?
items.a: Only the client. We receive no commissions from distributors, suppliers or professional firms, and we pay no commissions either. Each partner firm invoices you directly for its own work. It is the same reason no one would want a lawyer paid by the other side.

items.q: Analyses always end up costing more than the estimate.
items.a: We state our fee in advance, and it does not change as the work progresses. Our partner firms also give fixed quotes with the scope set out in writing. We must quote any additional work in writing and obtain your approval before it starts. We never price it after the event.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: We set out our own timescales in the proposal. No one can dictate the timetable of Brazilian authorities such as Anvisa, INPI or the courts, and we tell you that from the outset.

items.q: Could you tell us which companies you have worked for?
items.a: No. We do not provide references or client names, whether or not a confidentiality agreement is in place. This is the same assurance we give you.

sections.title: Questions you do not ask us, but that are worth asking

items.q: Is your trade mark registered in Brazil?
items.a: European registration does not protect your trade mark in Brazil. In Brazil, trade mark protection is obtained through INPI, the Brazilian National Institute of Industrial Property. As a rule, the right belongs to whoever files first. Someone else, possibly even one of your partners, may already have filed for it.

items.q: Is your product already on sale in Brazil without your knowledge?
items.a: It happens more often than you might think. Third-party sellers offer your product on Brazilian marketplaces and ship it from abroad. It pays to know who is selling it, at what price and with what guarantees for the consumer, because it is still your name on the product.

items.q: How much would it cost to end the contract with your commercial representative or distributor?
items.a: In Brazil, the law entitles a commercial representative to an indemnity when the relationship ends. For a distributor, the contract and the courts determine the outcome. You work out the cost of leaving before you sign, not after the relationship has soured.

items.q: Did you check your partner before signing?
items.a: It is possible to check a Brazilian company’s debts, ongoing legal proceedings and tax status. Many projects come to a standstill precisely because of problems with the partner, which a prior check would have brought to light.

items.q: In whose name is your product registered with the health authority?
items.a: For products regulated by Anvisa, the Brazilian health authority, the registration is held by a company based in Brazil. If that company is your importer, switching importers may mean starting the process all over again.

items.q: Which Brazilian state should your goods enter through?
items.a: Brazil is not a single market. The ICMS, the tax on the circulation of goods, varies from state to state, and some states offer incentives to importers. The choice of point of entry affects the final price.

sections.intro: Hardly anyone asks us these questions when they first get in touch. Yet the outcome often depends on them. We ask ourselves these questions from the outset.
